rationale: A wins because it treats the facts like live ammunition instead of decorative confetti: "Calm built 4 million paying subscribers. Its next 25 million users won't pay it directly" finds the business tension hiding in the update and asks the money question without inventing the answer. B has useful scaffolding, but "Health Insurers Start Covering Meditation Apps. The Wellness-to-Clinical Shift Is Arriving" overstates the clinical threshold, and its research-integrity angle drags in outside baggage the update never supplied. A is narrower, cleaner, and more pitchable.
gaps_in_A: The category angle still needs restraint around "coverage-line story" because the update says covered benefit, not reimbursable medical treatment; A mostly handles this, but the phrase edges toward overclaiming.
"expected or historical engagement rates Calm can share" is a fair proof ask, but if Calm cannot provide it, the member-use angle becomes a sidebar rather than a standalone pitch.
A could have pressed harder on the journal tier. It asks for the citation, but not whether the journal is serious enough for a clinical desk.
gaps_in_B: "Wellness-to-Clinical Shift Is Arriving" overclaims the supplied facts. Calm Premium as a covered benefit plus a self-reported anxiety study does not automatically make the app a clinical benefit.
"Coverage Was the Last Wall" is slogan-brained. The update does not say coverage was the final barrier, or that access, adherence, provider acceptance, or clinical validation are solved.

The contrarian angle invents too much outside scaffolding: "Health Researchers Recognize This Pattern," "pharmaceutical research, food science," and "funder effect persists" are plausible context, but they are not in the update and would require sourcing before becoming an angle.

Refusing "Business/revenue mechanics" is a miss. The undisclosed economics are exactly why a business-of-healthcare reporter might care; A correctly turns that hole into the story instead of throwing it away.
